extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and practicing patent attorneys handling equity suits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing practice, evidence, jury/feigned issues, pleadings, and proof in equity (chancery) proceedings for patent infringement. Focused on how and when juries/feigned issues are used, what evidence is admissible, burdens of proof, and procedural limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury trial in equity is discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: That a jury trial under Sec. 2, act of 1875, is matter of discretion not of right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity usually conducts inquiries within its own tribunals but may summon and impanel a jury of not less than five nor more than twelve persons to present issues it deems expedient and proceed upon their verdict as if tried at law. Submission of feigned issues to a jury is entirely within the court's discretion; no appeal lies from refusal, though an appellate court may remand for a jury trial when expedient.

rubrics_metrics.name: When feigned issues may be ordered
rubrics_metrics.description: A feigned issue may be allowed when the patent is recent, the novelty doubtful, the identity of the infringing process or device uncertain, and the proof conflicting or the credibility of witnesses disputed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feigned issues are less often used when the patent and infringement have already been established by a verdict or the patent has long exclusive possession. Courts grant jury issues especially where originality is doubtful or evidence is contradictory; they are not favored generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of verdict on feigned issues (advisory only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The verdict of the jury in a cause sent from chancery is advisory only and never conclusive; equity may disregard it and render a contrary decree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A motion for a new trial for a verdict against evidence must be made to the chancery judge; after verdict the defeated party may proceed in equity and introduce further evidence unless time for taking evidence has expired. If feigned issues are ordered before the time for taking evidence expires, the time will be extended until after the verdict and sufficient opportunity for additional testimony is afforded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence admissible in equity corresponds to law
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence admissible in equity upon the various issues created by the bill and answer is the same as that receivable at law upon the corresponding issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See applicable sections for particular issue-by-issue admissibility. General rule: rules of evidence correspond; statutory defenses requiring notice at law require the same notice in equity unless properly pleaded in the answer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in equity pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof rests upon the plaintiff as to all material averments of his bill, and upon the defendant as to matters of avoidance or estoppel or the subordination of a legal to his equitable rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff bears burden for damages and material allegations; the affirmant bears burden of proving an equitable title against a legal title and must plead accordingly (e.g., bona fide holder for value without notice must be specifically denied).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof on infringement and on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof on the question of infringement rests on the appellant, and if he fails in it the decree will be affirmed; where the defendant denies infringement the plaintiff must prove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement may be found from circumstantial evidence even if no direct act is proved. A single witness's testimony, with corroborating facts, can suffice when denial in answer is not positive and unequivocal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of admissions in the answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever is averred in the bill and not denied in the answer is admitted and need not be further proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An answer under oath responsive to the bill makes and proves the issue and requires two witnesses, or their equivalent, to overthrow it. An irresponsive answer is an admission; an equivocal answer (particularly on infringement) gives strong presumptions for the plaintiff; direct admissions are conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of defendant books vs confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may compel the defendant to produce the books by which infringing sales are evidenced, but cannot, under preliminary proof, force him to disclose the details of his business and give the names of confidential customers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will protect confidential business details; generally only such discovery as directly evidences infringing sales is compelled. In some instances plaintiff cannot compel more than one confidential customer's name under preliminary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office correspondence and originals in feigned issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Office copies of the plaintiff's correspondence with the Patent Office, as to the re-issue or its construction, are not admissible evidence on the trial of feigned issues unless properly sent with the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originals or office copies concerning reissue/construction should be sent down with the record to law court; otherwise they are inadmissible on feigned issue trials. Where feigned issues present no question of fraud or mistake and bill is based on a re-issued patent, the original is not admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depositions practice: time limits and examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: When testimony is taken by deposition the court fixes a period within which each party shall complete his evidence and appoints an examiner to receive testimony and transmit it to court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party fails to take evidence within the prescribed time and does not apply for extension, the court may proceed and determine the cause on the pleadings. Evidence taken after the appointed time will not be read at the hearing if the other party objects. When evidence is taken under special order, conformity with notice is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections must be timely, specific, and on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to evidence must be made when it is offered before the examiner and must be entered on the record of the testimony; each objection must state the specific grounds or those grounds are waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general objection is inadequate; failure to object at the proper time or to state grounds waives later complaint. If a party is present at examination and does not object, he cannot later take advantage of the defect on hearing or appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of evidence not objected to is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence not objected to can be employed only for purposes for which it is legally admissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, evidence taken without objection under a general denial of priority may be competent on final hearing both as to state of the art and priority but only for proper purposes; inadmissible-in-part evidence remains usable only to the extent legally permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use/prior invention evidence and notice rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior use taken without proper notice and objected to will be struck out; evidence offered late (after close of evidence) such as affidavits of public use may be too late and not regarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depositions of witnesses not named in the answer or taken without due notice are vulnerable; courts may allow evidence taken over objection in certain circumstances or if pleadings are amended and the opposing party not surprised. Courts exercise discretion, sometimes admitting evidence taken out of time if no prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavits and expert evidence timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits cannot be entitled in the cause before the bill is filed and affidavits not entitled in the cause are mere extra-judicial oaths and not receivable; application to put in expert evidence must be made before the first hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits not properly before the court are generally inadmissible. Expert evidence requests should be timely to permit inspection and fair opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence not presented to examiner generally cannot be used in argument
rubrics_metrics.description: No evidence can be used in argument before the court unless presented to the examiner and appearing on the record, except such documents as are equally accessible to both parties and whose connection with the controversy is so apparent that their production by one can operate as no surprise upon the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a document is equally accessible (e.g., public record) and obvious relevance, it may be used even if not on the deposition record; otherwise use requires transmission via the examiner and record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court discretion to strike/suppress evidence and allow amendment or rehearing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the record of the testimony with objections is returned to court the inadmissible evidence may be struck out, or if inadmissibility arises from want of proper averments the defects may be amended and the evidence then received, or the cause sent back to the examiner for repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may refer the record back to the examiner for additional evidence or re-examination for sufficient cause, limited to designated points; discretion commonly exercised where opposing party had full cross-examination and opportunity to rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination rights and limitations of witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent cannot be asked a question on the trial of a feigned issue if the reply would contradict an admission in his answer; a witness may decline to answer improper questions during deposition and refer objections to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party whose deposition is taken has right to decline answers deemed improper; questions that would contradict admitted facts are impermissible. Motions to suppress testimony because a witness was mistaken are generally not allowed if the examination was in due form and after due notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing after hearing requires leave
rubrics_metrics.description: After the hearing and submission neither party has the right to file any paper in the case without leave of the court, upon motion and due notice to the adversary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must obtain court permission and give notice before filing additional papers post-submission; the hearing record and briefs are the basis of decision unless court grants leave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity practice follows chancery and applicable court rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice in equity in actions for infringement follows that of the English chancery as it existed before the 'New Rules' were adopted, except where changed by express regulations; rules in equity prescribed by the Supreme Court are binding on the Circuit Court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity rules were framed to conduct the cause to a hearing; privileges conferred by the rules and objections for their violation must be made available before or during the hearing to preserve rights on appeal.
